title: The day I’ll never forget

fn.en: Talk about past experiences using the full range of past forms.

gr: the past simple, past continuous and past perfect together

can.en: I can tell the story of something that happened to me, in the right order.

rc: the present perfect against the past simple

acts.say: Tell the story of one of these in two sentences.

items.x: A medical team happened to be nearby.
He was stuck there for twenty-four days.
She reached the surface and took a breath.
Sadly, nobody was looking for her.

sub.en: Which past form does each part of the story need?

items.q: While he ___ for the path, he fell into a stream.
items.why: The past continuous sets the longer action that was already in progress.

items.q: While he was looking for the path, he ___ into a stream.
items.why: The past simple carries the short, finished event that interrupts it.

items.q: His phone did not work because he ___ it in the water.
items.why: The past perfect shows which of the two past events happened first.

items.q: By the time they found him, he ___ there for three weeks.
Teams of people ___ for him all that week.
items.why: The past continuous gives the background situation that ran through the story.

items.q: I ___ him twice since that day.
items.why: RECYCLED: since that day reaches up to now, so the present perfect is used.

items.q: I ___ him last April, and we talked for an hour.
items.why: RECYCLED: last April is finished time, so the past simple is used.

items.q: When we arrived, the ambulance ___ already.

sub.en: One story, three forms — read the timeline from the top down.

head.en: What it does in the story

rows: He had eaten at the restaurant on the mountain.
While he was looking for the path,
he fell into a stream and broke his leg.
Teams of people were searching for him.
They found him twenty-four days later.
I have never forgotten that story.

lines: It [was|had been|has been] an ordinary Saturday until about four o’clock.
While I [was walking|walked|had walked] home, I [noticed|was noticing|had noticed] smoke above the roofs.
By the time I got there, somebody [had already called|already called|has already called] the fire service.
Luckily the family [had left|left|were leaving] the building an hour earlier.
I [have thought|thought|had thought] about that afternoon many times since then.

items.from: First he dropped the phone. Then he tried to call for help.
items.a: When he tried to call he had already dropped the phone

items.from: He was walking down. Suddenly he fell.
items.a: While he was walking down he fell

items.from: The search lasted three weeks. Then they found him.
items.a: By the time they found him three weeks had passed

items.from: She left the house. After that the storm started.
items.a: She had left the house before the storm started

items.from: I have not been back since that day.
items.cue: Say when you last went — in 2019

items.from: He fell into the stream. Before that, he had eaten at the restaurant.
items.cue: Put it in one sentence with BEFORE. Begin: He had eaten…
items.a: He had eaten at the restaurant before he fell into the stream

items.from: I was cooking. At that moment the lights went out.
items.cue: Put it in one sentence with WHILE. Begin: While I…
items.a: While I was cooking the lights went out
alt: While I was cooking, the lights went out

items.from: They arrived at eight. The train left at half past seven.
items.cue: Use ALREADY + the past perfect. Begin: When they arrived…
items.a: When they arrived the train had already left
alt: When they arrived, the train had already left

items.from: I have not seen him since 2020.
items.cue: Rewrite it in the past simple. Begin: I last…
items.why: RECYCLED: since + present perfect for a period up to now; a finished point takes the past simple.

items.from: She started the job in March and she is still there.
items.cue: Rewrite it with FOR and the present perfect. Begin: She has…
items.a: She has worked there for months
alt: She has been there for months
She has worked there since March
She has been there since March

items.from: The dog ran away. Nobody ever found it.
items.cue: Rewrite the second sentence with NEVER. Begin: It was…

items.why: The longer action in progress takes the past continuous.
The earlier of two past events takes the past perfect.
A short, finished event takes the past simple.
last April is finished time, so the past simple is used.
for + a length of time; since + the point when it started.

tts: That reminds me of another story I heard about a man who had a lucky escape.
He had been at a barbecue restaurant on top of a mountain.
After the meal he decided not to take the cable car down with his friends, but to walk down instead.
While he was looking for the path, he fell into a stream and broke his leg.
He could not move. He tried to phone for help, but his mobile was not working, because he had dropped it in the water.
Teams of people were looking for him, but it was twenty-four days before they found him.
Luckily, he had brought a bottle of barbecue sauce with him, and he survived by drinking water mixed with the sauce.

items.sit: You are starting a story about something you still remember clearly.
o: I’ll never forget the day I lost my keys in the river.
I’ll never forget the day when I was losing my keys in the river.
I never forget the day I had lost my keys in the river.

items.sit: You want to say that one action interrupted a longer one.
o: While I was waiting for the bus, my phone rang.
While I waited for the bus, my phone was ringing.
While I had waited for the bus, my phone rang.

items.sit: You want to make it clear that the accident came before you arrived.
o: It had already happened when I got there.
It already happened when I had got there.
It has already happened when I got there.

items.sit: You want to mark the surprising turn in your story.
o: Suddenly, the lights were going out.
Suddenly, the lights had gone out and then they went out.

items.sit: You want to say that the whole thing ended well.
o: Luckily, nobody has been hurt yesterday.

items.sit: A friend asks whether you have been back to that place since.
o: No, I haven’t been back since that day.
No, I didn’t go back since that day.
No, I hadn’t been back since that day.

write.q: Write the story of a day you will never forget. Use at least one past continuous sentence for the background, two or three past simple sentences for the events, and one past perfect sentence to show what had happened earlier.
plan: where you were and what was going on
write.model: I’ll never forget the day our train stopped in the middle of nowhere. It was an ordinary February morning and I was reading by the window. Suddenly the lights went out and the train stopped. Nobody said anything for about twenty minutes. It turned out that a tree had fallen across the line an hour earlier, and the driver had been waiting for instructions. In the end we walked two kilometres along the track in the snow. Luckily, a bus was waiting for us at the road.

speak.q: Tell the same story out loud in about a minute. Do not read it — look at your plan and tell it.
speak.model: I’ll never forget the day our train stopped in the middle of nowhere. I was reading by the window when the lights suddenly went out. A tree had fallen across the line an hour before, so we sat there for twenty minutes and then walked two kilometres in the snow. Luckily there was a bus at the road.
